## Overview

The Lacandon are one of the Maya peoples living in the jungles of the Mexican state of Chiapas, near the southern border with Guatemala. Their homeland, the Lacandon Jungle, lies along the Mexican side of the Usumacinta River and its tributaries. Lacandon communities also occur in Betel, Lacanjá San Quintín, Lake Metzaboc, Metzaboc, and Najá. The Lacandon are among Mexico’s most isolated and culturally conservative Indigenous peoples. Their population is described as approximately 650 speakers of the Lacandon language in one source and as 1,000 Lacandon people in another. Lacandon is a Mayan language closely related to Yucatec Maya. The Lacandon are significant in folk-culture terms for their ritual houses, deity pots, incense practices, sacred relationships with Maya ruins, forest-based history, and continuing negotiations with outside influence.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name deity faces, straight or braided hair, and striped or checked designs on ritual pots.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide no complete account of everyday and ceremonial dress. They state that Lacandon clothing and personal adornments changed considerably between the late 19th century and later periods, and that historical photographs and drawings record this change. The sources also state that southern Lacandon had slightly different dress from their highland counterparts. Earlier scholars considered Lacandon appearance and dress similar to the ways ancient Maya represented themselves in murals and relief carvings. No specific garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named dress components are identified.

### Architecture

Most Lacandon villages have a God House where ceremonies take place. Some God Houses stand near the religious leader’s abode or near the home of a respected or elderly man; others are hidden in the jungle and guarded or shielded by vegetation so that outsiders cannot see the rituals. The building is constructed very low to the ground and oriented toward North, South, East, and West. Its entrance is on the east side, facing Maya ruins and the sunrise.

The interior contains drums suspended from the ceiling, benches, ceramic bowls, a conch shell used to announce ceremonies, and a large hollowed trough for making Balché. It also contains a fire starter, rubber characters, incense nodules made of copal, and ceramic God pots used to burn offerings. Sacred places include caves, Maya ruins, rivers, rock outcroppings, and particular places in the jungle where vegetation was not cut. These sites are often remote, secret, and not intended for outsiders.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The most fully documented objects are God pots: small ceramic bowls with the head and face of a deity attached to the rim. The head is often tilted backward so that incense or offerings can be placed directly on it. The pots are fired in the open, coated with clay, lime, and water, and painted with red or black dyes. Masculine and feminine forms are distinguished by features including straight or braided hair and striped or checked surfaces.

The Lacandon also made arrowheads from flint quarried in the rainforest and used bows and arrows into the 20th century. A fire starter traditionally consisted of a fire drill made from two sticks; lighters, matches, or flint were also used more recently. The sources mention metal tools as goods sought through trade and as objects associated with the god Äkyantho’.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They state that clothing and personal adornments changed considerably over time, and that photographs and drawings from the late 19th century record these changes. Some Lacandon formerly practiced bloodletting by cutting the earlobe or septum and smearing blood onto rubber figurines before burning them.

## Music & performance

The sources describe drums as ritual instruments. In the God House, drums are suspended from the ceiling so that they do not touch the ground until they are needed for ritual song and dance. A conch shell functions as a trumpet to announce the beginning of a ceremony to both villagers and the gods. Ritual ceremonies generally have male participants and may be performed for feeding a particular god, fertility, agriculture, or healing.

Lacandon ritual music and dance have decreased since ethnographers began studying the group, although the reasons are described as inexplicable in the source. Casa Na Bolom collaborated with Swedish ethnomusicology students who recorded traditional Lacandón songs, and a publication of those recordings in CD form was planned.

## Dance & theatre

They state that ritual songs and dances took place in the God House and that the use of music and dance decreased in ritual behavior over time. No theatre, mask performance, or named entertainment dance is documented.

## Festivals & rituals

Lacandon ceremonies usually have male participants and are held for various purposes, including feeding a god, fertility, agriculture, and healing. As disease increased through contact with outsiders, more rituals focused on healing. Basic offerings and incense burning are performed by male heads of household, while a man recognized for ritual knowledge, healing ability, or religious leadership may conduct ceremonies.

Offerings burned in God pots include incense, food, and rubber figurines. The figurines are made from sap of the Castilla elastica tree and commonly represent humans, although some represent animals. They are splattered with red annatto dye before burning. The smoke is understood as the essence or soul, pixan, consumed by the gods. The sources describe earlier bloodletting connected with these offerings and state that such practices were nonexistent or unknown by the 20th century.

God pots are considered alive and to have a soul. Small pebbles taken from Maya ruins give them life, while cacao beans provide a “heart.” Each pot is made for a particular deity or ritual. When a pot becomes full of incense, contains burnt offerings, or breaks, a renewal ceremony replaces it. The old pot is left in a sacred place, and new incense burners, figurines, and a pot are made.

The Lacandon also made pilgrimages to ancient Maya cities to pray and remove stone pebbles from ruins for ritual purposes. They believed that the Maya sites were places where their gods had once lived.

## Foodways

They state that ceramic bowls in the God House were used to prepare and eat ritual meals or offerings. A large hollowed trough was used to make the alcohol Balché for ritual consumption. Ritual food was thought to sustain the gods and maintain order in the universe.

The sources also state that polygyny helped retain ritual knowledge in food preparation and maintain fertility among wives at different times.

## Oral tradition & literature

They state that Christian missionaries from the Summer Institute of Linguistics worked with southern Lacandon to translate the New Testament and parts of the Old Testament into their language.

Christian Rätsch spent three years living with the Lacandon while studying their spells and incantations. Casa Na Bolom has sponsored research on Lacandon history and culture, returned copies of photographs and other cultural documentation, and collaborated on recordings of traditional Lacandón songs.

## Language & religion

Lacandon is a Mayan language closely related to Yucatec Maya. Lacandon speakers refer to themselves as *Hach Winik*, meaning “Real People,” and call their language *Hach T’ana*, “Real Language.” Another source gives the forms *Jach tʼaan* and *Hach tʼan*. Most Lacandon people speak Lacandon Maya, and most also speak Spanish. Lacandon has adopted words from Ch’ol and Tzeltal, and some Lacandon have developed distinctive styles of speaking Spanish.

Lacandon religion includes a pantheon of gods and goddesses, God Houses, sacred ruins, incense burning, ritual meals, God pots, rubber figurines, pilgrimages, and offerings. Named deities include K’akoch, Sukunkyum, Hachäkyum, Tuub, Ah Kin Chob, Mensäbäk, Hahanak’uh, Kisin, Ak K’ak’, Äkyantho’, and Hesuklistos. Southern Lacandon abandoned their pantheon in the 1950s and were later Christianized through the Summer Institute of Linguistics. Northern Lacandon religious traditions remained stronger around Lakes Naja and Mensabok, particularly through the leadership of Chan K’in, who died in 1996.
